messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ananya was thirty‑seven when the night in the dimly lit parking lot behind the grocery store became the turning point of her life. A quiet, single mother in a quiet New England town, she had always been the kind of woman who kept the lights on in her shop after hours, her shelves humming with the sound of her own quiet routine. When a man slipped a knife into her back, he was a stranger who looked like one of the men she had known on the street before, the same face she had seen on television in the news reports of similar assaults. That face—one that she would later notice in the crowd at the bus stop—was the first trigger that set the invisible chain in motion. Every time she sees a man whose features resemble that attacker, her mind snaps to the night of the assault. The thought that someone could come close to her again fills her with dread and forces her to avoid the very public buses that carried her to the store. She steers her car into the closest lane, pulls into the side street, and keeps her back pressed against the wall of the shop at all times. That avoidance itself reinforces the image of the attacker; the more she hides from the bus, the more she recalls the night, and the more vivid the memory becomes in her mind. She can’t articulate the terror; the words elude her, but she knows the scene: the cold metal of the knife, the smell of his breath. Each flash of the memory pulls her back into a state of panic, and the sudden movement of people in the street—an unexpected hand, a quick turn of a shoulder—makes her feel that she is again in the assault, on the brink of being caught by a hidden blade. The memories are not merely images. When she hears the name of the victim on the radio, a deep wave of guilt washes over her. She believes, with a certainty that blinds her to the reality of her own right to move on, that she somehow deserves what happened. The guilt is tied to the terror she feels when she remembers the event; the two are inseparable, a loop that spins faster with each thought. The more she ruminates on how life might have been different—“if only I had stayed at home, if only I had not left the shop on that evening”—the more the memory dominates her day. Her counterfactual thinking pulls the event into her present, making it feel as though the night still looms over her daily life. Her avoidance has begun to erode the very life she had built. The shop’s sales have dipped; her husband, a schoolteacher, has been too stressed to come home early to help. Ananya has started to be overly compliant with the shop’s new security system, fawning over every suggestion from the manager because the idea of confrontation is now more terrifying than a locked door. When a customer asks about a promotion, she answers politely and then quickly deflects the conversation to other topics, a pattern that seems to ease her nerves but also isolates her from the community she once loved. Over the past year, Ananya has felt as if she is trapped in a room with her back to the wall, always looking for the outline of a safe space. She is convinced that a single careless movement by another person could trigger a flashback, that the next bus she misses could mean a new assault. The terror of her memory has become a constant undercurrent, and every trigger—from a similar face in the crowd to a mention of her ex—sets her mind racing toward the night, the threat that feels both impossible and imminent. The cycle is tightening; each avoidance reinforces the memory, the memory fuels the threat, and the threat brings her back to the triggers. It is only this relentless loop that finally pushed her to seek help. Ananya’s fear has become a burden that she can no longer carry alone; she worries that the shop will close, that her husband will leave, and that her own safety will remain compromised. In the present moment, she sits on the back of a chair in the shop’s small break room, looking out at the window where she can see the street from a safe distance, and she thinks that she deserves to feel safe again. The most immediate hope is to break the chain that has made her life feel like a series of threats, and the most profound fear is that she may never find a way out of this ever‑tightening spiral.
